title: HTTPS & TLS: The Handshake Handbook
summary: A dense field guide to how HTTPS actually works — TLS 1.2 and 1.3 handshakes step by step, certificate chains and validation, SNI, session resumption, and the metadata encryption leaves exposed. Covers internals, real-world usage, trade-offs, and the misconfigurations that bite in production.

chapters.title: What HTTPS Actually Is
points: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS; no change to HTTP semantics, only the transport is wrapped
TLS sits between TCP (L4) and the application layer — application writes plaintext, TLS encrypts records
Default port 443 for HTTPS vs 80 for plaintext HTTP; port choice is convention, TLS is not port-bound
SSL is the dead ancestor: SSL 2.0 (1995), SSL 3.0 (1996), both broken and disabled; 'SSL' persists only as a colloquial name and in library names (OpenSSL)
TLS version timeline: 1.0 (1999), 1.1 (2006), 1.2 (2008, RFC 5246), 1.3 (2018, RFC 8446). TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated by RFC 8996 in 2021
Three guarantees TLS provides: confidentiality (eavesdropper can't read), integrity (tamperer can't modify undetected), authentication (server proves identity)
Authentication is usually one-way: server proves who it is, client stays anonymous unless mTLS is configured
TLS gives no guarantee about the server's honesty — a valid cert on phishing-site.com is still valid; it proves domain control, not trustworthiness
Record layer: after handshake, data is chopped into records (max 16 KB plaintext each), each independently encrypted and MAC'd/AEAD-sealed
Handshake protocol vs record protocol: handshake negotiates keys, record protocol carries bulk data using those keys
Hybrid crypto: asymmetric (slow, RSA/ECDHE) used only to agree on keys; symmetric (fast, AES/ChaCha20) used for all bulk data
Cost model: handshake is the expensive part (1–2 round trips + asymmetric math); steady-state encryption is near-free with AES-NI hardware instructions
`https://` in the browser bar means 'encrypted and the cert validated', not 'safe site'
Mixed content: an HTTPS page loading an HTTP script gives an attacker full control of the page — browsers block active mixed content outright

chapters.title: The TLS 1.2 Handshake, Step by Step
points: Precondition: TCP 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) already completed — TLS starts on an established stream
Step 1 ClientHello: client sends max TLS version, 32-byte client random, session ID, list of cipher suites in preference order, and extensions (SNI, ALPN, supported curves, signature algorithms)
Step 2 ServerHello: server picks ONE cipher suite and version from the client's list, sends its own 32-byte server random and session ID
Step 3 Certificate: server sends its leaf certificate plus intermediate CA certs (chain order matters, root is normally omitted)
Step 4 ServerKeyExchange: for ECDHE suites the server sends its ephemeral public key, signed with the cert's private key — this signature is what proves the server holds the key
Step 5 ServerHelloDone: signals server is finished with its half
Step 6 ClientKeyExchange: client sends its ephemeral public key; both sides now compute the same ECDHE shared secret
Step 7 Key derivation: pre-master secret + client random + server random run through the PRF to yield the master secret, then session keys (separate encryption and MAC keys per direction)
Step 8 ChangeCipherSpec + Finished: each side flips to encrypted mode and sends a Finished message containing a hash of the entire handshake transcript
The Finished message is the anti-downgrade check: if an attacker edited any earlier plaintext handshake message, the transcript hashes diverge and the handshake aborts
Cost: 2 full round trips (2-RTT) before the first byte of application data — plus 1 RTT for TCP = 3 RTT to first byte
Cipher suite string decoded: `TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_GCM_SHA256` = ECDHE key exchange, RSA authentication, AES-128-GCM bulk cipher, SHA-256 for the PRF/handshake hash
Static RSA key exchange (client encrypts the pre-master secret to the server's RSA public key) has no forward secrecy and is removed in TLS 1.3
Gotcha: everything through ServerHelloDone is plaintext — the certificate and SNI are visible on the wire in TLS 1.2

chapters.title: TLS 1.3: What Changed and Why
points: 1-RTT handshake by default: client guesses the server's key-share group in ClientHello, so keys can be derived one round trip earlier
ClientHello now carries `key_share` (an ephemeral public key) speculatively; if the server wants a different group it sends HelloRetryRequest, costing an extra RTT
EncryptedExtensions: everything after ServerHello — including the certificate chain — is encrypted, so the server's cert is no longer visible to passive observers
Cipher suites shrank to 5, and only name the AEAD + hash (`TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`) — key exchange and authentication are negotiated separately in extensions
Removed for good: RSA key transport, static DH, CBC-mode ciphers, RC4, 3DES, MD5/SHA-1 signatures, compression, renegotiation, and custom DHE groups
Forward secrecy is mandatory — every TLS 1.3 handshake uses ephemeral (EC)DHE, no exceptions
AEAD-only: all cipher suites are authenticated encryption (AES-GCM, AES-CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); no more encrypt-then-MAC vs MAC-then-encrypt footguns
HKDF replaces the TLS 1.2 PRF; a key schedule derives distinct secrets per handshake stage (early, handshake, application) so a leak at one stage doesn't unlock others
0-RTT (early data): client resumes and sends application data in its very first flight — zero round trips to first byte
0-RTT's price: early data is replayable, because the server has no fresh randomness in it yet. Only send idempotent requests (GET, not POST)
Middlebox compatibility mode: TLS 1.3 sends a dummy ChangeCipherSpec and fakes the TLS 1.2 version field so broken middleboxes don't drop the connection
Downgrade protection: server puts a magic sentinel in the last 8 bytes of ServerRandom when negotiating a lower version, which the client checks
Comparison row — RTT: TLS 1.2 = 2, TLS 1.3 = 1, TLS 1.3 resumption + 0-RTT = 0
Comparison row — cert visibility: TLS 1.2 plaintext, TLS 1.3 encrypted
Migration reality: TLS 1.3 was designed to be deployable over the existing internet, which is why the wire format still cosplays as TLS 1.2

chapters.title: Certificates: Structure and Contents
points: X.509 v3 is the certificate format; a cert is a signed statement binding a public key to an identity
Core fields: version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer DN, validity window (notBefore/notAfter), subject DN, subject public key info, extensions
The CA signs a hash of the TBSCertificate (to-be-signed) blob — modifying any field breaks the signature
Subject Alternative Name (SAN) is the field that actually names the hostnames. Browsers have ignored Common Name (CN) for hostname matching since ~2017
SAN types: dNSName (most common), iPAddress, and rarely email/URI
Wildcard certs match exactly one label: `*.example.com` covers `api.example.com` but NOT `example.com` itself nor `a.b.example.com`
Key Usage vs Extended Key Usage: KeyUsage says digitalSignature/keyEncipherment; EKU says serverAuth (1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1) or clientAuth — a cert without serverAuth is rejected for HTTPS
Basic Constraints: `CA:TRUE` plus a pathLenConstraint marks a CA cert; a leaf must be `CA:FALSE` or an attacker could mint certs from it
Encodings: DER is binary; PEM is base64 DER wrapped in `-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----`. `.crt`/`.cer`/`.pem` can be either; `.p12`/`.pfx` bundles cert + private key
Validation types: DV (proves domain control, minutes, free), OV (org vetted), EV (extended vetting). Browsers removed the EV green bar — EV now buys essentially no UI benefit
Certificate lifetimes keep shrinking: 825 days → 398 days (2020) → 47 days (industry ballot, phasing in through 2029). Manual renewal is no longer viable; automate with ACME
SCTs (Signed Certificate Timestamps) embedded in the cert prove it was logged to Certificate Transparency; Chrome rejects public certs without them
Inspect with: `openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text` and check the live chain with `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host`
Self-signed cert = issuer equals subject, signed with its own key. Fine for internal tooling with an explicitly trusted root, never for the public web

chapters.title: Chains, Roots, and Trust Stores
points: Chain shape: leaf (your server) → one or more intermediate CAs → root CA. Trust flows down, verification walks up
Roots are self-signed and live offline in an HSM; intermediates do the day-to-day signing so a compromise doesn't burn the root
The root is NOT sent on the wire — it must already be in the client's trust store. Sending it wastes bytes
Path building: the client picks the leaf, finds an issuer whose Subject matches the leaf's Issuer, verifies the signature, repeats until it hits a trusted root
At each hop the client checks: signature validity, notBefore/notAfter window, basicConstraints CA:TRUE, pathLen not exceeded, and revocation status
Trust stores are per-platform, not universal: Mozilla NSS (Firefox), Microsoft, Apple, Android, and each has its own inclusion policy and update cadence
The weakest-link problem: any CA in any trust store can issue for any domain. ~150 roots means ~150 organizations can mint a cert for your site
Certificate Transparency (CT) is the mitigation: every publicly trusted cert must be published to append-only logs, so mis-issuance is detectable after the fact
Monitor your own domains with crt.sh or a CT-monitoring service — that's how you find a cert someone else got for your name
Cross-signing: a new root gets signed by an established root so old devices still chain successfully. One cert, two valid paths
The Let's Encrypt DST Root X3 expiry (Sept 2021) broke old Android and OpenSSL 1.0.2 clients — classic example of a chain that validates on new clients and fails on old ones
#1 production misconfiguration: forgetting to serve the intermediate. Browsers often paper over it via AIA fetching / cached intermediates; curl, Java, and Go clients hard-fail
Revocation is the broken part: CRLs are huge, OCSP is a privacy leak and fails open (a soft-fail check an attacker can just block)
OCSP stapling fixes the privacy and latency problem — the server fetches its own signed OCSP response and staples it into the handshake. `Must-Staple` in the cert makes it non-optional
Short lifetimes are winning over revocation: a 47-day cert is its own expiry mechanism

chapters.title: Hostname Verification and What Clients Must Check
points: Two distinct steps clients conflate: (1) is the chain cryptographically valid and trusted, (2) does the cert actually belong to the host I dialed
Skipping step 2 is the classic silent vuln — a valid cert for attacker.com passes chain validation on a connection to bank.com
Match the SAN dNSName entries against the hostname from the URL, not against the IP or the redirect target
Wildcard matching rules: leftmost label only, no partial-label wildcards (`ap*.example.com` is not accepted), never matches across a dot
IP-address connections need an iPAddress SAN; a dNSName entry does not cover an IP literal
Trailing-dot and IDN/punycode edge cases: `example.com.` and Unicode homograph names are frequent bypass sources

Danger patterns to grep for: `verify=False` (Python requests), `InsecureSkipVerify: true` (Go), `-k`/`--insecure` (curl), `rejectUnauthorized: false` (Node), a TrustManager whose `checkServerTrusted` body is empty (Java)
Each of those disables authentication entirely — the connection is still encrypted, but to whoever answered, which is exactly the attacker's position
The right fix for a self-signed internal CA is to ADD the CA to the trust store, not to turn verification off
Certificate pinning: hard-code an expected leaf or intermediate key hash. Stops a rogue-CA attack, but bricks your app if you rotate keys without shipping a backup pin
HPKP (HTTP public key pinning) was the web version and is dead — too easy to permanently brick a domain. Mobile apps still pin, carefully, with backup pins and a kill switch
HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) tells browsers to refuse plaintext to this host for `max-age` seconds — closes the initial http:// redirect window an attacker can hijack
HSTS preload list ships in the browser binary, protecting even the very first visit; getting removed takes months, so `preload` is close to a one-way door
mTLS flips it around: the server sends a CertificateRequest and the client presents its own cert. Standard for service-to-service and zero-trust internal networks

chapters.title: SNI: One IP, Many Sites
points: The chicken-and-egg problem: the server must send a certificate before it knows which site the client wants, because the HTTP `Host:` header comes after the handshake
SNI (Server Name Indication, RFC 6066) solves it: the client puts the target hostname in a ClientHello extension so the server can pick the right cert
Pre-SNI the workaround was one IP address per HTTPS site — a real constraint that shaped early hosting prices
SNI is what makes shared hosting, CDNs, and cloud load balancers possible: thousands of certs behind a single IP
SNI is sent in PLAINTEXT even in TLS 1.3 — it's in ClientHello, before any keys exist
Consequence: your ISP, your employer's proxy, and any on-path observer sees exactly which hostname you visit, even though the page content is encrypted
SNI-based blocking is deployed at national and corporate scale precisely because it's cheap: read one field, drop the packet
ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) encrypts the real ClientHello — including SNI — under a public key published in the domain's HTTPS DNS record, sending a decoy 'outer' SNI in the clear
ECH only helps if many domains share the same outer name and key (an anonymity set); a lone ECH-enabled origin is still identifiable
ECH's dependency chain: you need encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) too, or the DNS lookup leaks the hostname before TLS even starts
Domain fronting was the old hack — a benign SNI with a different `Host:` header inside. Major CDNs killed it by requiring the two to match
SNI mismatch gotcha: send the wrong or no SNI and you get the server's default cert, producing a confusing hostname-mismatch error. `openssl s_client -servername` exists for exactly this
Debug it: `curl -v --resolve example.com:443:1.2.3.4 https://example.com/` pins the IP while keeping SNI and Host correct
Server config: nginx `server_name` selects the virtual host by SNI; the first `server` block for a listen address is the fallback when SNI doesn't match anything

chapters.title: Session Resumption and Handshake Performance
points: Motivation: a full handshake costs round trips and asymmetric crypto. Resumption reuses an earlier session's secret to skip both
Session IDs (old way): server stores session state in a cache keyed by a 32-byte ID, client echoes it in ClientHello. Stateful — doesn't scale across a server fleet without a shared cache
Session tickets (RFC 5077): server encrypts the session state into an opaque blob and hands it to the client to store. Stateless server, scales horizontally
The ticket key is the crown jewel: it encrypts every ticket. Leak it and an attacker decrypts every session that used it, retroactively destroying forward secrecy
So: rotate ticket keys frequently (hours, not months), and keep them in memory. Many defaults never rotate — that's the trap
In TLS 1.3 resumption is PSK-based: the server sends `NewSessionTicket` after the handshake, which the client uses as a pre-shared key next time
Resumption is 1-RTT in TLS 1.3; adding `early_data` makes it 0-RTT
0-RTT replay: an attacker can capture and re-send early data because the server contributed no freshness. Servers must restrict early data to idempotent requests or maintain an anti-replay window
Add `psk_key_exchange_modes` with (EC)DHE to resumption to restore forward secrecy — pure PSK resumption has none
TLS False Start (TLS 1.2 era) let the client send data right after its Finished, shaving an RTT — largely superseded by TLS 1.3's 1-RTT
The other big lever is connection reuse: HTTP keep-alive and HTTP/2 multiplexing mean one handshake amortizes across hundreds of requests
OCSP stapling also saves an RTT and a DNS lookup that the client would otherwise spend contacting the CA
Measure it: `curl -w '%{time_appconnect} %{time_connect}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com` — the delta is your TLS handshake cost
Session resumption is also a tracking vector: a ticket is a unique identifier a server can correlate across visits, which is why browsers scope and expire them per-site

chapters.title: What Encryption Does NOT Hide
points: Leaked in the clear: destination IP address and port — routing requires it, always visible
Leaked: the DNS query for the hostname, unless you use DoH or DoT
Leaked: SNI in ClientHello, unless ECH is deployed on both ends
Leaked in TLS 1.2 (not 1.3): the entire server certificate, which names the site outright
Leaked: ALPN, revealing whether you speak HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or HTTP/3
Leaked: packet sizes, timing, and direction. Traffic analysis on this alone identifies which page of a site you loaded, which video you streamed, and which app you're using
Leaked: total bytes transferred and connection duration — enough to fingerprint distinctive workloads
Leaked: JA3/JA4 client fingerprints derived from the ordering of cipher suites and extensions in ClientHello — identifies your TLS stack, and often the specific app or bot
Encrypted: URL path and query string, HTTP headers, cookies, request and response bodies. These are inside the tunnel
But 'encrypted in transit' ≠ 'secret': URLs with tokens in the query string land in server logs, browser history, `Referer` headers, and analytics pipelines
TLS protects the wire only. The server decrypts everything — TLS says nothing about what happens to your data afterward
Corporate TLS interception: an enterprise installs its own root CA on managed devices, and the proxy decrypts and re-encrypts everything. Fully visible traffic, and the padlock still shows
Free wifi captive portals do the same trick when they can get you to install a profile — the padlock is not evidence of privacy on a managed device
The metadata summary: TLS hides WHAT you said, not WHO you talked to, WHEN, HOW MUCH, or HOW OFTEN

chapters.title: Failures, Fixes, and the Field Checklist
points: Historic attacks and their lessons: BEAST (2011, CBC IV reuse), CRIME/BREACH (compression + secrets = oracle), Heartbleed (2014, OpenSSL memory disclosure leaking private keys), POODLE (2014, SSL 3.0 padding), FREAK/Logjam (2015, export-grade downgrade), ROBOT (2017, RSA padding oracle again)
Common thread: nearly every one exploited a legacy feature or a downgrade path. TLS 1.3 deleted those features rather than patching them
Error triage — `certificate has expired`: check `notAfter`, check server clock skew; a wrong client clock produces identical symptoms
Error triage — `unable to get local issuer certificate`: the intermediate isn't being served, or the client's CA bundle is stale. Fix the chain, don't disable verification
Error triage — `hostname mismatch`: the SAN doesn't cover this name; often actually a wrong-SNI or wrong-vhost problem
Error triage — `handshake failure` with no detail: usually no overlapping cipher suite or TLS version between client and server
Error triage — `self signed certificate in certificate chain`: a corporate MITM proxy is on the path; add its root to your trust store deliberately
Config checklist: TLS 1.2 + 1.3 only, ECDHE-only key exchange, AEAD ciphers only, disable renegotiation and compression, enable OCSP stapling
Serve the full chain (leaf + intermediates, no root), and prefer ECDSA certs with an RSA fallback for old clients
Set HSTS with a real `max-age` (≥1 year), `includeSubDomains`, and `preload` only once you're certain every subdomain is HTTPS
Automate issuance with ACME (certbot, lego, caddy, cert-manager) — with 47-day certs, manual renewal is guaranteed downtime
Alert on expiry at 14 days, not 1 day, and monitor CT logs for certs you didn't request

Tools: `openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host` for the raw handshake, `testssl.sh` for a full local audit, SSL Labs for a graded external report, Wireshark to watch a handshake byte by byte
Rotate session ticket keys, keep private keys off disk backups, and treat a leaked private key as a full-site compromise requiring revocation plus reissuance

The one-paragraph summary: TLS wraps TCP to give confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication; certificates chain a hostname to a trusted root; SNI tells the server which cert to send and leaks the hostname doing it; resumption trades a little forward secrecy for a lot of latency; and the tunnel hides content while broadcasting metadata
